faq: Is BotLoadout free?
Yes. All 97 templates are $0 and the archive downloads without payment. The site is funded by newsletter sponsorship, and sponsorship bookings do not open until January 2027.
What do I actually get with a template?

One page per job, with separate Claude, ChatGPT and Grok prompts, the connectors to enable, setup steps, an example input and output, and the template's limits. There is no hosted agent: you paste the prompt into your own account.
Can I use the templates at work?

The terms allow personal and commercial use, including work accounts, with no attribution. The only restriction is reselling or republishing the library, or a substantial part of it, as a competing template collection.
trial_checklist: Run one template against a real task, your own inbox or a live lead list, rather than a sample prompt. Check three things: whether the connectors it asks for exist in the account you actually use, whether the example output matches the format you need, and how much editing the draft needs before it is usable. Record time to first useful output and the number of edits, then run the other platform's version of the same template on the same task. Treat the limits section as the vendor's own statement, not a tested result.
rating_rationale: Job fit 4 - 97 templates cover a broad spread of first-agent jobs and each states its connectors, example output and limits, which is more than most prompt libraries offer. Output quality 3 - the prompts are structured and documented, but unverified: nothing has been independently tested and results depend on the reader's own model and connectors. Adoption 4 - free, no account and a public archive make the start cost close to zero. Cost 5 - there is nothing to buy. Trust 3 - operator, licence and privacy notice are now published and specific, but the site is two weeks old with no track record. Weighted to 3.9.

faq: How much does Robylon cost?

Starter is free with 300 credits a month (roughly 40 conversations). Pro starts at $25/month for 500 credits, rising through $75, $113 and $158 at 1,500, 2,500 and 3,500 credits. Business starts at $180/month for 4,500 credits up to $300 for 10,000. Yearly billing takes 10% off. Enterprise is quoted. Live-agent seats are optional and cost $19 to $89 per seat per month. Check the official pricing page before buying.
Do I need live agent seats to use Robylon?

No. Many customers run AI agents only. Seats are for teams that want to answer escalations inside Robylon's own inbox; on Business and Enterprise the agent hands unfinished work to Freshdesk, Zendesk or Zoho Desk instead.
What happens when credits run out?

AI agent replies pause until credits are added, while the live-agent inbox keeps working. Robylon notifies you at 50%, 20% and zero balance. You can buy extra credits at $25 per 1,000, or move to a higher credit tier.
Robylon vs Intercom or Zendesk?

Robylon lists a conversation at roughly $0.20-$0.38 against Intercom's reported $0.99 per Fin resolution and Zendesk's roughly $1.50-$2.00 per committed resolution. Robylon's figure is per conversation attempted rather than per resolution, so it is not a like-for-like comparison. Model your real volume before choosing.
trial_checklist: Connect one helpdesk or the standalone inbox and one knowledge source, then replay a week of real resolved tickets through the agent and read the ones it closed without a human. Check the credit burn at your actual conversation volume rather than the plan's estimate, since voice calls use credits at a different rate to chat and email. Ask what is retrievable from the trust centre before you rely on the SOC 2 Type II or HIPAA claims, and confirm the deletion window you need.
rating_rationale: Job fit 5 - the job is resolving support conversations rather than answering them, and the product is built around acting through API-built tools and handing off with checks done. Output quality 4 - the vendor publishes specific customer-reported automation rates (85% chat, 80% ticket resolution, over 95% knowledge-base queries) and a named SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA posture, but the cited trust centre returns HTTP 403, so the compliance evidence is stated rather than inspectable. Adoption 4 - self-serve signup with no card, a free tier, public documentation and a published integration list, from a named California entity on a domain registered in January 2024. Cost 4 - $0.20-$0.38 per conversation undercuts per-resolution rivals, but the headline voice and WhatsApp channels sit on Business from $180/month and all payments are non-refundable. 4.3 because provenance and the self-serve path are unusually strong while the compliance evidence surface is not publicly readable.

The scale claims are unverifiable and implausible for the domain's age: "200K+ users" and "10M+ images" on a domain registered 2026-08-30, about seven and a half weeks before this check

There is no self-serve account deletion or data export - both are email requests to the same address - and the public config endpoint shows password reset and email verification both disabled, so an unverified address can hold an account with no recovery path

The free tier is promised on the pricing page ("Free $0 forever", "5 free credits", "No credit card required") while the Terms hedge it: complimentary credits "exist only if the operator enables them in configuration" and "These Terms do not promise a daily free generation"

Paid credits expire 365 days after purchase and consumed credits are not refundable, so a light user can lose unused balance with no coded expiry reminder (the Terms say so: "This product does not send a coded expiry reminder")
The blog linked in the main navigation is empty: "No posts yet - check back soon"

Payments run through Waffo Pancake, a processor most buyers will not recognise, and the site publishes nothing about card brands, chargeback handling or dispute escalation beyond naming it as PCI-DSS compliant

The Terms say "the public catalog lists 1K as the supported resolution" while llms.txt describes 1K/2K/4K choices in the generator "where the selected model and credit balance allow them" - confirm which tiers actually deliver 2K or 4K before paying for an upscale
key_features: Browser editor: upload an image, give a natural-language instruction, pick a model, aspect ratio and output count, review and download

Dedicated tool pages for the AI image upscaler (2x/4x/8x), the object remover, photo restoration and GPT Image 2.5
Reference images and masks for prompt-based editing rather than prompt-only generation
Credits wallet with one-time packs and 365-day validity; no subscription tier
Prompt screening before generation and output-image moderation before delivery, both fail-closed with credits restored
Google sign-in and Google One Tap enabled, plus GitHub sign-in per the privacy policy
English, Simplified Chinese and Traditional Chinese locales across pricing and every legal page
Five free credits on sign-up with full-resolution downloads and no card required
faq: How much does Retouchia cost?

Five free credits on sign-up, then two one-time packs: Basic at $9.99 for 350 credits and Pro at $29.99 for 1,200 credits, both valid 365 days. There is no subscription. The cards advertise the packs against $12 and $39.90 anchors at 16% and 24% off, and the en, zh and zh-tw pricing pages carry the same figures. Unused credits from a pack are refundable within 7 days; consumed credits are not.
Is there a subscription?

No. The Terms say "We sell one-time credit packs only. We do not offer subscriptions", and the Refund Policy repeats it. Credits expire 365 days after purchase and the site does not send an expiry reminder.
Which AI models does it use?

This is the part to check before you buy. The Terms and the Acceptable Use Policy name SparkPix (model IDs sparkpix-image and sparkpix-image-edit on APIModels) and Nano Banana 2 (gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview on APIMart, nanobanana2 on APIModels). The navigation on every page and a dedicated landing page instead advertise GPT Image 2.5 and call it "OpenAI's" model, and no legal page mentions GPT or OpenAI, and no page carries an OpenAI non-affiliation statement.
Does it train on my images or prompts?

It says no: the Terms state it "does not use your Input to train models unless you give separate, explicit consent", and note that the product has no training-opt-in control - so there is no training by default. The input licence is limited to processing your file to run the service.
What happens to my uploads?

Reference assets expire after 1 hour and generated results after 7 days, both removed by a scheduled Cloudflare cleanup, and the policy is explicit that an expired result URL does not necessarily delete the underlying record. Prompts, generation records and stored result URLs are kept until you request deletion by email. There is no self-serve delete or export.
Who owns the images I generate?

You do. Terms section 9 says AI images generated from your prompts belong to you and may be used for any lawful purpose the Acceptable Use Policy allows, while the Retouchia name, software and marks stay with the site.
Can I get a refund?

In three cases: a pack with none of its credits used within 7 days, a duplicate charge from a billing error, or an EU/UK/Australian first-purchase withdrawal right exercised before first use. Consumed credits are not refunded. A failed or blocked generation restores credits, which the site states is not a money refund.

name: TheFaceRating
best_for: Anyone who wants a fast, private read on facial proportions before spending money on a haircut, a pair of glasses or a colour palette, and who reads the score as a styling starting point rather than a verdict on attractiveness. Also a useful sandbox: the Studio scores any reference photo against your own face. Not a fit for readers who want the rating to mean something objective, who need a working support mailbox before they pay, or who would rather not involve a face at all - the free scan keeps the photo on the device, but the colour analysis and every try-on require sending a compressed copy to the vendor and its model providers.
price: Free on-device scan with no account. Paid reports are one-time purchases, not subscriptions: Starter USD 7.99, Pro USD 16.99, VIP USD 24.99, listed identically on the homepage plan cards, the results-page paywall and Terms section 6. Studio credit packs are stated in the Terms only - 10 credits for USD 9.99 and 30 credits for USD 19.99, one credit per rating plus render, credits do not expire. Checkout is a live Stripe session (verified 2026-10-24: cs_live session for 'TheFaceRating Starter Report' at USD 7.99, merchant Vban LLC, Apple Pay and Google Pay offered); applicable tax shows at checkout. Free AI colour analyses are capped at two per day per hashed IP address.
summary: TheFaceRating turns one selfie into a face rating. Google's MediaPipe face mesh places 478 landmarks in the browser, the site levels the head on the iris line and scores 11 proportions into a single 0-100 harmony number, then names the face shape across six prototypes and shows symmetry, canthal tilt, facial thirds and width-to-height ratio against a reference band. It also returns a celebrity bone-structure 'twin' as a percentage. The free scan needs no account, and we confirmed by running it that the measuring step sends nothing: landmarks, ratios and the result page are produced with no outbound request. The paid report adds 14 try-on renders on the buyer's own photo - six hairstyles, four necklines, four eyewear frames - plus a 12-season colour palette, a styling guide and, on Pro and VIP, a 30-day plan, a PDF and Studio credits for rating any look you find. Colour analysis is the one step that needs the photo, and the site asks for it with an unticked consent choice that can be declined while still returning full geometry results. Reports are sold by Vban LLC, a Wyoming company, under Wyoming law.
use_cases: Getting a facial-proportion readout - face shape, symmetry, canthal tilt, thirds, fWHR - without an account or an upload
Choosing between haircuts, frames or necklines before paying for one, using the face-shape classification first and the rendered try-ons second
Building a 12-season colour palette from a selfie instead of booking an in-person draping session
Testing whether a specific hairstyle, outfit or pair of glasses found online suits your face, one Studio credit per look
Creating a styling plan for a specific event or a wardrobe refresh, with a 30-day schedule on the Pro and VIP reports
pros: The privacy claim is behaviour, not copy: we ran the free scan on the vendor's own sample photo in a logged browser and the page made no outbound request while it measured - 478 landmarks, the 0-100 score and the full results page were produced with the network untouched

The one step that does send data is gated by an explicit choice rather than a pre-ticked box: after the free result the site offers 'Continue with color analysis' or 'Skip - geometry results only', each labelled with what happens to the photo, and choosing Skip still produces a complete result page and a scannable report

What leaves the device on that path is only a sha256 hash, the geometry object and the celebrity match - the POST body we captured carried no photo field at all, which matches the policy's claim that only derived measurements are received

Legal documentation is well above the category: a biometric-specific privacy policy with a retention table (uploaded selfies 2 hours, free results 48 hours, paid reports and renders 12 months, consent records 3 years, hashed IP counters 24 hours), processors named by company with what each one receives (Google Gemini for colour and try-ons, OpenAI for text only, Cloudflare for hosting, database and private storage, Stripe for payments, Resend for mail), a no-training commitment and a 'never sell, never advertise' statement

The operator is named and contractually located - 'Vban LLC', Sheridan, Wyoming, governing law and forum in Wyoming - which most submissions in this catalog do not manage, and the policy is written to double as a BIPA/CUBI retention and destruction policy while citing GDPR, UK GDPR and CCPA rights

Pricing is one-time and agrees on three surfaces: homepage cards, the results-page paywall and Terms section 6 all read USD 7.99 / 16.99 / 24.99 with 'no subscription', and the paywall opens a live Stripe session at the stated amount

Framing of the number is honest: the example result is labelled as an AI-generated model and not a real person, the FAQ says outright that a face rating is not an objective measure of attractiveness, and the footer repeats 'not a medical or psychological assessment' - no testimonial wall, no countdown timer, no before/after claims

The Terms put real limits on how the tool may be used: no rating, mocking or identifying other people, no uploading someone else's photo without permission, no photos of under-18s, no deceptive use of renders, and output use limited to personal non-commercial purposes with social sharing allowed
The alternative guides name the competing products - TheFaceReport, Umax, Qoves, PinkMirror, FaceIQ Labs - instead of pretending the category starts with this site
cons: The only addresses the site publishes are dead: privacy@thefacerating.com, used for rights requests, deletion and refunds, cannot receive mail because thefacerating.com carries no MX record at all, so a buyer whose report fails has no published route to the seller

The refund promise lives as one paragraph in Terms section 7 and depends on that same dead address; there is no refund page in the sitemap, and a /refunds page search engines still index now returns 404

Analytics load before any consent choice: GA4 (G-VGC2RBRR2T) is preloaded and configured inline on first paint, so EU and UK visitors get _ga cookies with no banner. IP anonymisation and ad-signal opt-outs are genuinely set, and the policy discloses the cookies, but disclosure is not consent
A Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon loads on every page and is not named anywhere in the privacy policy, which lists Cloudflare for hosting, database and private file storage only

'Vban LLC' could not be confirmed in a public company search, and the published Sheridan address is a registered-agent block shared by many companies, so the entity is named in full but its registration is unverified from outside

The score is a geometry formula on a single photo: the site itself warns that lighting, angle and lens change the result, and the 'Top 2%' band labels attached to a strongest feature are the scanner's own reference set, not a published percentile

Plans can only be compared after a scan - the nav's Pricing link goes to a homepage anchor, there is no standalone pricing page, and the Studio credit packs (10 for USD 9.99, 30 for USD 19.99) appear in the Terms rather than in any purchase interface we could reach

Biometric-adjacent by design: even with a genuinely local free scan, colour analysis and every try-on require sending a compressed copy of a face to the vendor and to Google Gemini, and paid measurements and renders are retained for 12 months
key_features: 478-landmark MediaPipe Face Landmarker running in the browser, with head-tilt levelling on the iris line before any measurement

Face-shape classification across oval, round, square, heart, diamond and oblong, returned with a confidence figure
Celebrity bone-structure 'twin' presented as a percentage match
Paid report with 14 identity-locked try-on renders on the buyer's own photo: six hairstyles, four necklines, four eyewear frames
12-season personal colour analysis behind an unticked consent step that can be declined
Studio: upload any hairstyle, neckline, outfit or glasses photo for a compatibility score plus a render on your face, one credit per look
Separate free tools for each measurement - face shape, attractiveness, PSL score, symmetry, golden ratio, canthal tilt, jawline, side profile, photo picker, celebrity structure
Result page with per-measurement reference bands, a shareable story card and a 48-hour expiry on free results
One-time report plans at USD 7.99 / 16.99 / 24.99 with a 30-day plan and PDF on Pro and VIP
faq: Is the free face rating actually free, and does it upload my photo?

Both parts check out. No account is needed, and when we ran the scan in a logged browser the measuring step made no outbound request at all - the 478 landmarks, the score and the full results page were produced with the network untouched. The next step, which saves the scan behind a link, posted only a sha256 hash of the image, the geometry object and the celebrity match. A photo is uploaded only if you accept the separate colour-analysis consent or buy a report.
What do the paid reports cost?

USD 7.99 for Starter, 16.99 for Pro and 24.99 for VIP, each a one-time payment with no subscription or auto-renewal. The same three prices appear on the homepage cards, on the results-page paywall and in Terms section 6, and the paywall opens a live Stripe session at that amount with Vban LLC as merchant. Studio credits are sold separately, 10 for USD 9.99 or 30 for USD 19.99 according to the Terms.
What happens to my face data?

The free scan is local. If you consent to colour analysis, or buy a report, a compressed copy (at most 1280 pixels on the long edge) goes to Cloudflare storage and to Google Gemini for the colour season and try-on renders; OpenAI receives text only, never the photo. Uploaded selfies are deleted within 2 hours, free results within 48 hours, paid reports and renders 12 months after purchase, and the policy states the data is never sold, never used for advertising and never used to train models.
How seriously should I take the score?

As a styling prompt, not a verdict. The number is a weighted average of 11 geometric proportions, each scored against a classical reference band, and the site itself says lighting, angle and lens change the result and that attractiveness is broader than geometry. The 'Top 2%' labels on individual features come from the scanner's own reference set; no percentile methodology is published.
Can I get a refund, and who do I contact?

Terms section 7 promises to fix a report or render that fails and to refund it if it cannot be fixed, and preserves your statutory consumer rights. The catch is the contact route: every address the site publishes is on thefacerating.com, and that domain has no mail exchanger, so privacy@thefacerating.com does not accept mail as of our 2026-10-24 check. Until the vendor publishes a working mailbox, treat the purchase as one you may have to resolve through the address they used to submit the site.
Can I use it on someone else's photo?

No. The Terms require you to upload only photos of yourself or of an adult who has given permission, bar photos of anyone under 18, and forbid using the service to rate, mock or identify other people or to deceive with the generated images. Renders may be shared on social media but are licensed for personal, non-commercial use.
trial_checklist: Run the free scan first and take the 'Skip - geometry results only' path: it returns the full measurement breakdown without sending the photo, which is the cheapest way to judge whether the formula describes your face at all
Use a front-facing, evenly lit photo with the forehead and jawline visible - the site warns that angle, lens and lighting move the number, so one photo is one reading, not a stable measure
Read the reference bands next to each measurement rather than the single 0-100 headline, and compare the sub-scores to see which proportion is actually dragging the total
Decide consciously about the colour analysis: accepting it is what sends a compressed copy of your face to the vendor and to Google Gemini, and declining still leaves you with the geometry report

Compare the three plans on the results page, not in the nav - there is no standalone pricing page - and check whether the VIP Studio credits are looks you will actually use before paying the extra USD 17

Before paying, note that the published refund route (privacy@thefacerating.com) had no working mailbox on 2026-10-24; if a render fails, contact the vendor through the address they submitted the site with and keep the receipt

rating_rationale: Job fit 4.2/5 - the core job is done properly and quickly: one selfie, no account, a real 478-landmark measurement rather than a black-box 'AI score', eleven named proportions with reference bands, face shape, and a paid layer that renders the recommendations on the buyer's own face instead of showing stock photos. The Studio generalises it to any look a reader finds. It is held below 4.5 by scope and by evidence: the score is one photo of geometry with no independent validation, the percentile labels are the vendor's own bands, and the paid report is a rendering bundle rather than something a reader could not assemble from the free tools plus a stylist. Transparency 4.0/5 - this is one of the better-documented submissions we have reviewed: a biometric-specific policy with a real retention table, processors and models named with what each receives, a no-training commitment, an 18+ rule, named statutory regimes, a named company with a postal address and a stated governing law, one-time pricing that agrees on three surfaces, and a live checkout at the advertised amount. The privacy claim also survived an actual run: nothing left the browser while the free scan measured, and the consent path is a genuine choice. The 4.0 is the remaining gap between what the site says and what it does at the edges - every published contact address is on a domain with no MX and therefore bounces, the refund promise depends on that address, GA4 sets cookies before any consent choice, and the Cloudflare analytics beacon loads without being named in the policy.

name: CCC (Claude Command Center)
best_for: Developers who already run several coding agents and keep losing track of them in terminal tabs. CCC is worth a look if you launch Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and friends from a terminal and want one local board that shows every session, which one is waiting on you, and which has quietly run out of context - without routing your work through someone else's cloud. It is not a fit for a single-session user (a terminal is enough), for anyone who wants a hosted team product with accounts and permissions, for a Windows or Linux shop expecting parity with the macOS app, or for a buyer who needs a company entity and a governing-law clause before installing software.
price: Free: USD 0, with no tiers, no paid plan, no seat count and no account for the local app. Licensed FSL-1.1-MIT (copyright 2026 Amir Fish), which is source-available rather than OSI open source: you may use, copy, modify and redistribute it for any Permitted Purpose, a Competing Use is barred, and each version converts to the MIT license on its second anniversary. Downloads are a 3.6 MB notarized and Apple-signed DMG, a Homebrew tap (amirfish1/tap/ccc), a curl installer for macOS/Linux and a PowerShell installer for Windows. The optional CCC Cloud phone relay is account-based; no price appears for it on any fetched page either. No page on the site carries a price token other than $0.
summary: CCC (Claude Command Center) is a local dashboard for people running several coding agents at once. Instead of owning execution, it reads each engine's on-disk state as the source of truth, so a session you started in a terminal, resumed by hand or launched headless outside the dashboard still shows up on the board - that is the difference between a dashboard and a second place you have to remember to work from. On top of the board it adds a needs-attention lane that flags sessions ending on a real question, a per-session context meter, plan-usage and rate-limit projections, a Kanban with a project tree and an infinite Flow canvas, group chats between agents, a work queue with verify-to-close receipts, git worktrees per task, and an optional fallback that keeps a limit-hit session running on a $0 model. The stack is deliberately plain: a stdlib-only Python server bound to 127.0.0.1 and a no-build vanilla-JS UI, with readable JSON state under ~/.claude/command-center/. Claude Code is first-class; Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Kilo Code, Kimi Code, OpenCode and Devin spawn and ingest with documented gaps. Version 5.39.0 shipped 2026-10-18 and the repository was pushed the same day this review was written.
use_cases: Seeing every coding-agent session on one machine, including ones started or resumed by hand in a terminal
Spotting the agent that asked a question forty minutes ago, or the one whose context window is nearly full
Arranging a fleet of sessions by stage - Working, Review, a testing column, Verified, Archived - instead of one flat list
Typing a follow-up into a dormant session from the browser and having it resume to receive it
Running a queue of tickets overnight with agents that claim, fix, verify and close work with a receipt
Keeping work going past a plan's usage limit by falling back to a free model, then switching back at reset
Watching the fleet from a phone over Tailscale rather than exposing a dashboard to the open internet
pros: The telemetry claim survives reading the code rather than only the copy: ccc_server/fleet_jobs.py documents the complete beacon payload field by field (schema_version, version, platform, and two booleans derived from the local last-run date), lists what is never sent - no install id, no prompts, transcripts, tool calls, session counts, token counts, repo paths, hostname, git config or IP - and CCC_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 is a hard kill switch that stops every byte rather than a preference stored somewhere

The richer opt-in daily ping was retired on 2026-09-28 and the code says so in the same comment block, with the reason (the consent banner was not worth the number, and active_seconds_today was broken by construction) - a vendor deleting its own telemetry surface and documenting why is rare

Site analytics are deliberately configured rather than left on defaults: PostHog is initialised with persistence memory, person_profiles identified_only, and autocapture, pageleave, session replay, surveys, dead clicks, performance, heatmaps and exception capture all off, with respect_dnt on, so pageviews and the download button are the whole measurement

The vendor publishes a threat model instead of a security page of adjectives: SECURITY.md names the absence of authentication, the loopback-only bind, the same-origin POST check, the fact that headless sessions run with --dangerously-skip-permissions, and that state files are created with the default umask (world-readable on macOS) with chmod 700 recommended on a shared machine

Data boundaries for the account-based surfaces are written down with periods rather than adjectives: CCC Cloud stores your email and consent records, paired devices as opaque IDs with a hashed credential, notification records for 30 days and a per-device audit log for 90 days, never uploads transcripts, paths or code, and exposes a closed five-capability list with no generic shell execution

Engine support is stated with its gaps instead of implying parity - Claude Code first-class, the other seven spawning and ingesting 'with documented gaps' - and the site lists the limitations of its own comparison table

The core mechanism is the interesting part: because each engine's on-disk state is the truth, a session survives closing the dashboard and a hand-resumed session is not invisible, which is the failure mode of orchestrators that want to own execution

Real distribution rather than a launch-page promise: 202 stars and 25 forks on a repository created 2026-04-13, a 3.6 MB notarized and Apple-signed DMG that resolves, a working Homebrew formula, a read-only demo on seeded data, a full changelog, and independent third-party write-ups plus a YouTube walkthrough
Free with no upsell ladder: no account, no seat count, no feature held behind a paid tier, and every release becomes MIT-licensed after two years

Bounded cost behaviour in the free-model path: a spawn that cannot reach the local free-model router refuses to start rather than silently billing, and the vendor documents that free runs strip ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KEY from the child process
cons: No privacy policy and no terms page: /privacy, /terms, /privacy.html, /terms.html and /legal/ all return 404 on ccc.amirfish.ai, and the operator's parent domain amirfish.ai publishes none either - the actual data practices live in the repository's docs/telemetry.md, SECURITY.md and docs/cloud-relay/SECURITY-AND-PRIVACY.md, which the footer links as 'Telemetry' and 'Security', so a reader has to follow a code link to learn what leaves the machine

No controller identity and no governing-law clause: the licensor is a named individual (Amir Fish, copyright 2026) with a personal site naming Sunnyvale, California and a LinkedIn profile, but there is no company, postal address, jurisdiction, dispute or liability forum anywhere for a buyer to rely on

The site loads PostHog from us.i.posthog.com on every page and no page on the site names the processor - the disclosure exists only inside docs/telemetry.md, which the analytics script points at in a code comment

An anonymous usage beacon is on by default and fires at most once a day with no identifier, but the only way to turn it off is the CCC_TELEMETRY_DISABLED environment variable; there is no in-product toggle or first-run notice

The security posture is honest but sharp-edged: the server has no authentication, it reads your Claude Code transcripts, and its headless spawns use --dangerously-skip-permissions, so anything that can reach the port can run arbitrary commands as your user; state files land world-readable by default and the vendor's own advice is to chmod 700 on a shared machine

FSL-1.1-MIT is source-available, not open source: redistribution as a Competing Use is barred until each version's second anniversary, and GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, so the MIT conversion is time-boxed per release rather than immediate
macOS-first: the DMG is the first-class path, Linux is headless, Windows runs through a PowerShell script, and seven of the eight engines are documented as partially supported

'Claude Command Center' is a crowded name - at least five unrelated GitHub repositories use the identical repository name (nubbymong, Dicoangelo, sorlen008, afstkla, adamclark64) - so searching for it returns several different dashboards; the brand here is CCC at ccc.amirfish.ai
The comparison against claude-squad, Conductor and Sculptor is vendor-authored and dated 'as of July 2026', so it is the vendor's own reading of a fast-moving category rather than an independent test
The site ships no sitemap.xml, no robots.txt and no llms.txt (all three 404), so discovery depends entirely on the GitHub repository and search
One maintainer, eight open issues and a very fast release cadence (5.39 in October on a project started in April), which means features you build a workflow around can move under you
key_features: One local board for every coding-agent session on the machine, read from each engine's on-disk state rather than only from sessions the dashboard spawned
Needs-attention lane for sessions that end on a real question, including plain-prose ones, with desktop notifications on macOS
Per-session context meter with warning and danger levels and one-click compact

Work queue with claim, fix, verify and close lifecycle, a queue-health watcher, and receipts that close GitHub issues with a commit-SHA comment

faq: How much does CCC cost?

Nothing. The local dashboard is free at $0 with no tiers, no paid plan and no account, and the license (FSL-1.1-MIT) permits use, copying, modification and redistribution for any purpose other than building a competing product, with each version converting to MIT on its second anniversary. The optional CCC Cloud phone relay is account-based, and no price for it appears on any page fetched during this review.
Is CCC really local, and what does it send home?

The app is local: it runs a stdlib-only Python server bound to 127.0.0.1 and keeps readable JSON state in ~/.claude/command-center/. It does send one anonymous beacon at most once per day containing the schema version, the app version, the platform string and two booleans saying whether this is the first beacon of the ISO week and of the month - no identifier, no prompts, no transcripts, no paths, no token or session counts. CCC_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 turns it off entirely. The website itself loads cookieless PostHog with memory-only persistence and no autocapture.
Can I run it on a team or a shared machine?

Not safely as a shared service. The server has no authentication and no per-user accounts: anything that can reach the port can spawn sessions and, because headless spawns use --dangerously-skip-permissions, can run commands as your user. The vendor's advice is loopback only, or a trusted private network such as Tailscale, and chmod 700 on ~/.claude/command-center/ on a shared machine. For a team, treat it as a per-developer tool, not a control plane.
Which coding agents does it actually support?

Claude Code is first-class. Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Kilo Code, Kimi Code, OpenCode and Devin spawn and ingest with documented gaps, and the site says so rather than implying uniform support. The macOS app is the most complete path; Linux is headless and Windows installs through a PowerShell script.
Do I need to hand over my Claude subscription or API key?

No. CCC runs your installed claude command, which reads its own login, and the vendor's docs/tos-boundary.md says the login token is never sent to the free router, another provider, CCC telemetry or another machine, and is never copied between machines. Free-model spawns strip ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_KEY from the child process first.
trial_checklist: Install from the notarized DMG or brew install amirfish1/tap/ccc, then chmod 700 ~/.claude/command-center/ before you use it on any machine you share - the vendor's own SECURITY.md says the state files land world-readable by default

Decide about the beacon before first launch rather than after: set CCC_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 if you want zero wire bytes, then read the payload list in docs/telemetry.md so the decision is based on the contract, not the marketing line

Test the central claim first: start a session in a terminal by hand, then open the board and confirm it appears without having been spawned from the dashboard - if hand-started sessions do not show up, the product is not doing the thing it exists for
Run one real task end to end and wait for the needs-attention lane to fire on a plain-prose question; that detection, not the Kanban, is what saves the wasted afternoon

Read every Agent config change in the consent dialog before approving it: CCC writes hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/hooks.json to get the sidecar state it reads, and it asks per change
Do not expose the port. There is no authentication; if you want it on your phone, use the Tailscale path or the outbound-only Cloud relay rather than binding 0.0.0.0
Keep the free-model fallback deliberate - choose '$0 Free' per session instead of setting 'Always' - so a limit hit cannot quietly route work to a different provider's model
Before relying on the work queue overnight, run it once on a scratch repository with three tickets and check that verify actually closes with a commit-SHA receipt rather than a summary
rating_rationale: Job fit 4.4/5 - it is the only tool in this category we found that treats each engine's on-disk state as the source of truth, which is the difference between a fleet board and a second place you have to remember to work from; the needs-attention lane, context meter and limit fallback address failure modes that cost real afternoons, and the stack is deliberately auditable (stdlib Python, no-build UI, readable JSON state). It is held below 4.5 by reach rather than by quality: macOS-first with Linux headless and Windows scripted, one maintainer, seven of eight engines partially supported, and a user base that is developers running many agents rather than the broader catalogue reader. Transparency 4.0/5 - the documentation is unusually strong and it survives inspection: the beacon payload is listed field by field in source with a hard kill switch, a richer opt-in ping was retired and the code says why, the site's PostHog config is coded to the minimum, and SECURITY.md names its own sharp edges including --dangerously-skip-permissions and world-readable state files. The 4.0 is the missing legal surface: there is no privacy policy and no terms page on ccc.amirfish.ai or on the parent domain, no company, postal address or governing-law clause, and the analytics processor is named only inside a repository document rather than on any page a reader would land on. Nothing in the documentation contradicts the product, which is why it lands at 4.1 rather than lower.

price: Starter free (25 gear items, 10 categories, 25 AI actions a week, one 50 MB client gallery, a 3-page site); Pro $4/mo or $39/yr; Studio $19/mo or $179/yr; no free trial on paid plans
summary: A camera-specific inventory and studio-operations app: every body, lens, filter, drone and accessory gets a record with serial number, purchase details, condition, storage location, photos, receipts and warranty files, plus loan status and service history. On top of that sit shoot planning with sun and weather, packing and readiness checks, QR labels and scan check-out, value trends and an insurance-ready PDF, and - on Studio - a client CRM, booking, quotes, contracts and invoices. An assistant called Iris answers questions about your own kit, including lens-to-camera mount compatibility, and a free browser tier covers 25 items with export on every plan.
use_cases: Building an insurance-ready record of a kit with serials, receipts and current values before something goes missing
Tracking which lens, body or light is on loan to whom, and what is due back or due for service
Packing a shoot from gear you actually own, with call sheets, sun times and weather
Running a small studio's gear calendar, check-outs and maintenance alongside client jobs and invoices
Comparing a spreadsheet against a camera-aware tool without paying first
pros: The operator is named inside the notice rather than left to a footer: privacy section 1 gives Dylan Andersen, GearDex, 842 St Vincent, Irvine, CA 92618, and the same identity appears on the legal notice and the contact page, with California as the governing law in the Terms

Every processor is named with its purpose and what it receives - Supabase for database, auth and files; Stripe for billing; Resend for transactional email and client replies; Vercel for hosting; PostHog and Google Analytics for analytics; NVIDIA for the AI features; Tavily for web lookups; Google for Calendar; Google reCAPTCHA on the contact form

The analytics behaviour matches the written claim: Google Analytics (G-BNVX42Q1BT) is loaded with Consent Mode defaulting analytics_storage and ad_storage to denied and send_page_view false, and the policy says Analytics runs only after you accept analytics cookies - with a working Accept All / Reject All banner and no analytics cookies or storage until you choose

Prices agree across three independent surfaces on the same day: the Offer array in the pricing page's structured data (0, 4, 39, 19, 179), the plan cards and full limit-by-limit comparison table, and the billing policy which restates $4/$39 and $19/$179 - and the site's llms.txt matches

The AI data flow is described precisely instead of hedged: what context reaches NVIDIA for Iris chat, Smart Add, receipt reading and the scheduled Pro/Studio suggestion job, that existing serials are not sent for receipt matching and are left out of suggestions, and that NVIDIA's own terms allow it to improve its models with request content - a limit the policy states GearDex does not control

Billing is written for the buyer rather than for the vendor: no free trial stated plainly, cancellation from Settings to Billing or the Stripe portal, a 14-day past-due grace period, how proration behaves, and a California Automatic Renewal Law notice

The legal set is complete and internally consistent - /legal/privacy, /legal/terms, /legal/billing and /legal/notice all serve, and the Terms' cross-reference to /legal/billing resolves rather than 404ing

It is a shipped product with surfaces to audit: the domain was registered 2025-06-28, /download lists Mac 1.3.0 and Windows 1.2.0 with in-app updates, and there is a public issue tracker and notarised release feed at github.com/dylandersen/geardex-public
Export is first-class on every plan, including the free one: a full account ZIP with records plus uploaded photos, receipts and documents, JSON records, or CSV for all gear or one gear type

Client money never passes through GearDex: invoices and deposits use the photographer's own Stripe, PayPal, Venmo, Square, Cash App or any https payment link, and the Terms say GearDex is not a party to the client agreement
cons: No iOS or Android app ships, although the privacy policy describes both three times - 'the GearDex apps for iPhone, Android and desktop', 'The iPhone and Android apps also ask before Iris first sends anything to NVIDIA', 'The GearDex apps for iPhone and Android don't include analytics' - while /download offers Safari's Add to Home Screen for iPhone, lists no Android app, and no App Store or Play link appears anywhere on the site
Retention carries no number: the policy says data is removed or anonymised 'within a reasonable period' of account deletion, with no stated window for photos, receipts, backups or analytics

On Pro and Studio a scheduled AI job sends brand, model, specifications, condition and purchase price to NVIDIA on its own schedule whether or not you ever open Iris; only Starter escapes that if you never start an AI feature
Iris chat context can include serial numbers, purchase prices, condition and storage locations sent to NVIDIA, whose terms permit using request content to improve its models
AI is metered weekly rather than generously: 25 actions on Starter, 150 on Pro, 'unlimited' with footnotes on Studio, and market price lookup capped at 10 a week on both paid plans
The free tier is a real ceiling - 25 gear items, 10 categories, 3 shoot plans, one 50 MB gallery, one gear document and one kit on your site - so a working kit of any size lands on Pro quickly

Refund position is thin: no free trial, refunds 'not automatic', and the billing policy's money-back guarantee is conditional ('we may offer a time-limited money-back guarantee... where such a guarantee is offered') while the pricing page advertises none, so a buyer should not assume a 30-day window exists
The submission labelled this 'Writing & Productivity', which does not describe the product; it is a gear-inventory and studio-operations app and is listed under Productivity
Solo operator - one developer in Irvine, a stated 1 to 2 business day support window, and phone support still described as 'coming to Studio plans'

Usage claims are the vendor's own and unverified by us (300+ photographers, 6,100+ items tracked, $722K+ managed), and one product page still calls the desktop app 'early access' and names Macs only while /download ships Mac 1.3.0 and Windows 1.2.0
No affiliate or partner programme is published - /affiliates and /partners return 404 - so there is no commercial relationship to disclose today
key_features: Camera-specific records with per-type spec fields (mount, sensor, megapixels for bodies; focal length, aperture, filter size for lenses; FAA registration and Remote ID for drones)
Serial numbers, purchase details, receipts, warranties and item photos attached to each record, with warranty expiry alerts
Loans and check-outs with QR labels, scan in and out, due and overdue reminders, and signed loan agreements
Maintenance history, recurring service schedules and issue flags
Shoot planning with shot lists, call sheets, sun and moon times, weather and backup plans
Packing and production-readiness checks built from gear you actually own
Value tracking, six- and 24-month trends, depreciation method choice, and a one-click insurance PDF
CSV import with per-type templates and row-level validation; ZIP, JSON or CSV export on every plan
Iris assistant for plain-English questions about the kit, including lens-to-camera mount compatibility

Studio tier: client CRM, pipeline inbox, online booking, quotes, contracts with e-signature, invoices via your own payment link, 10-seat team workspace, and the Studio Agent API with webhooks and an MCP adapter
faq: How much does GearDex cost?

Starter is free with up to 25 gear items in 10 categories, 3 shoot plans, one 50 MB client gallery, one gear document and 25 AI actions a week. Pro is $4 a month or $39 a year; Studio is $19 a month or $179 a year. A year of Pro saves $9 against twelve monthly payments and a year of Studio saves $49. The pricing page's structured data, the plan cards and the billing policy all carry the same figures.
Is there a free trial on the paid plans?

No. The billing policy states plainly that GearDex does not offer a free trial on paid plans, and that the free Starter tier is the way to evaluate it. Refunds are also not automatic once a billing period has begun, and the money-back guarantee clause is conditional rather than advertised on the pricing page.
Can GearDex replace a gear spreadsheet?

For a working kit, largely yes: the record holds serial, receipt, value, condition, location, documents, loan status and service history, and a CSV import brings an existing list across with row-level validation. What it adds over a spreadsheet is gear-specific structure - mounts, warranty expiry, loans, maintenance - and what it does not do is appraise your gear: recorded values are your own figures, and the site says plainly that it does not provide insurance or guarantee a claim.
What does GearDex do with the photos and serial numbers I upload?

Inventory data, including serials, purchase prices, values and receipt files, is stored in the account in the United States with Supabase. AI features send a request to NVIDIA only for Iris chat, Smart Add, AI descriptions, receipt reading, and a scheduled suggestion job on Pro and Studio; the policy lists what each one includes, that existing serials are not sent for receipt matching, and that NVIDIA's terms allow it to improve its models with request content. Starter inventory is not sent unless you start an AI feature.
Does GearDex take a cut of client payments?

No. Invoices and deposits are paid through the photographer's own payment link with Stripe, PayPal, Venmo, Square, Cash App or any https link, and the Terms state that GearDex is not a party to the client agreement, so disputes and chargebacks sit between the photographer, the client and that provider.
trial_checklist: Start on Starter with ten real items rather than a full import: include two similar lens names, one adapter, one borrowed item and one body in for repair, then check that Smart Add keeps model, quantity and ownership distinct and that a deliberately ambiguous model name gets a question rather than a guess. Export once and re-import to confirm serials, purchase dates and documents survive the round trip. Then plan one real shoot and compare your own packing list against GearDex's - mark omitted batteries, wrong mounts and anything flagged unavailable - and ask Iris one compatibility question you can verify against the manufacturer. Only after that does the paid question arise: whether Pro's unlimited items, own domain and 150 weekly AI actions remove work you are actually doing, or whether 25 items was enough.
rating_rationale: Job fit 4.3/5 - camera-specific records with the fields that matter for a real kit, receipts and warranties beside the item, loans, maintenance, shoot planning and a working export on every plan, held back by a 25-item free ceiling and weekly-metered AI. Transparency 4.1/5 - the notice names the controller, a postal address and every processor with purpose, analytics runs behind Consent Mode defaulting to denied with an honest Accept All / Reject All banner, prices agree across the structured data, the cards and the billing policy, and the legal set is complete with a resolving cross-reference. Two things keep it off 4.5: the policy describes iPhone and Android apps that do not ship, and retention has no stated window. Overall 4.2 - the top of the range for a product we have not tested, because the disclosures are verifiable rather than merely present.

name: HumanPen
best_for: Writers and researchers who already have a finished Word or PowerPoint file and need the file itself changed - AI phrasing reduced, references converted to a target style, a document cut to a word limit, or a layout-preserving translation - then downloaded again as an editable DOCX or PPTX. The unit of work is a whole document, not pasted text, so it suits a 50,000-word thesis with cross-references and figure numbering. Not a fit for anyone who wants a draft written for them (there is no generation entry point), for non-English humanizing, for assessed work where the institution restricts AI assistance, or for a buyer who needs a named company, country, postal address or a governing law that names a jurisdiction.
price: Pay-as-you-go credits, one-time purchase, no subscription: 1,000 credits USD 19, 5,000 USD 79 (marked most popular), 10,000 USD 149, 20,000 USD 249. Every account's first purchase is discounted to USD 9.90 / 49 / 98 / 196 for the same four packs, once per account. New accounts get 100 free credits. Credits never expire and work in the web app and the API. Humanizing costs 100 credits per 1,000 words actually rewritten; citation-format correction is the cheapest operation at 5 credits per 1,000 words. Checkout runs through Waffo (the Privacy Policy also names Creem), each acting as merchant of record; prices are USD and no recurring plan is sold - the Terms state each purchase is a one-time charge.
summary: HumanPen is a document toolbox that works on files rather than on a text box. You upload a DOCX or PPTX and get the same format back, edited: an AI-phrasing rewriter with two strengths that can import your own Turnitin or iThenticate report and touch only the flagged passages, a citation-format converter covering 12 styles, a shortener that hits a target word count, and a translator for 12 languages that keeps layout, charts and formulas. Billing is metered - you are charged for words actually rewritten, not for the whole file - and credits do not expire, so a 500-word job costs cents instead of a month's subscription. The humanizer is English-only and the vendor says so. There is also a documented REST API, an MCP server and an agent skill. The site is candid to an unusual degree about what the tool is for: the /ethics page states plainly that the humanizer is used to lower detector scores, declines to promise a pass, declines to run its own detector, and the Terms forbid submitting work as your own where an assessment requires independent work.
use_cases: Rewriting AI-drafted passages inside a thesis or report while keeping citations, tables, figure numbering and Word fields intact
Importing a Turnitin or iThenticate report so only the flagged passages are rewritten and only those words are billed
Converting an entire reference list and in-text citations to APA 7, MLA 9, Harvard, IEEE, Chicago, Vancouver, AMA, ACS, OSCOLA or GB/T 7714 in one pass
Cutting a manuscript to a submission word limit without breaking structure or references
Translating a PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX or EPUB between 12 languages with charts, formulas and page layout preserved
Running the same four operations over many files through the documented REST API, MCP server or agent skill instead of one paste at a time
pros: Genuinely document-level: input and output are the same editable format, and the vendor's stated design rule - numeric values, units, percentages, statistical notation, exhibit numbering, in-text citations and reference entries are protected during a rewrite - is the thing a paste-based humanizer cannot do

Billing matches the job: 100 credits per 1,000 words actually rewritten, so importing a detection report and rewriting only the flagged passages costs a fraction of the document, and a second pass on still-flagged passages is free

The commercial model is clean and verifiable: four one-time packs whose prices agree across the rendered pricing page, the site's public packages endpoint and the page metadata, credits that do not expire, and a Terms clause stating each purchase is a one-time charge with no renewal anywhere

Refund terms are specific rather than decorative: full refund within 14 days on an untouched purchase, credits removed on refund, automatic credit return when a job fails on their side, and an explicit note that consumer-protection rights are not limited
Output ownership is stated in the user's favour - you retain rights to input and output, no ownership claim is made, and the licence to process ends when the content is deleted

The /ethics page is the most honest document in this category that we have read: it concedes the humanizer exists to lower detector scores, refuses a detected-or-refunded guarantee, refuses to run its own detector on the grounds that grading your own exam is not persuasive, and says outright that a processed manuscript still counts as AI-assisted for disclosure purposes

Retention is given as periods and tied to a mechanism - uploaded documents and results deleted 7 days after the job finishes, account deletion within 30 days, payment records kept 7 years - and the site says the 7-day window is enforced by a scheduled sweep rather than by hand
A real developer surface, documented rather than promised: a published OpenAPI 3.1 schema, a machine-readable API guide, an MCP server and an agent skill, so the same operations run in a script
cons: Advertising trackers the privacy policy does not disclose: Google Ads gtag AW-18511954133 and a Microsoft Ads UET (bat.bing.net) tag are injected in the root layout with lazyOnload and fire on every page, including /legal/privacy itself, with remarketing and conversion requests to google.com/rmkt/collect and googleadservices observed - while Privacy Policy section 10 says cookies are only those 'necessary to sign you in and keep the Service working' and 'We do not use them to build advertising profiles', and section 5's processor list mentions no Google or Microsoft

No consent mechanism at all: there is no cookie banner, no consent-mode call and no way to refuse the ad tags on a site that receives uploaded manuscripts - the policy's section 4 talks about consent as a legal basis the site relies on elsewhere, but nothing on the page asks for it

No operator identity and no named jurisdiction: the Terms are accepted by 'the HumanPen team', the About page says only 'built and maintained by the HumanPen team', and the governing-law clause is circular - 'the laws of the jurisdiction in which the HumanPen team operates' - so no country, company, company number or postal address appears on any page

The product is marketed at graded coursework while its own Terms forbid academic dishonesty: /humanize/homework-assignment prices 'a 500-word assignment' and pitches discussion-board posts as text that should 'read like something you typed off the cuff', and /business-solutions sells bulk humanizing to institutions - against Terms section 6, which bars submitting work as your own where an assessment requires independent work. The vendor's stated position is that the institution sets the rules and the user answers for the use; readers in assessed work should treat this as a policy risk, not a study aid

Effectiveness is unverifiable from outside and the vendor does not claim otherwise - there is no pass-rate figure, no third-party test, and no detector of its own to check against, so the only honest expectation is that the wording changes and the AI involvement does not

Humanizing is English-only, citation correction and condensing accept DOCX only, and only Turnitin and iThenticate reports can be imported - three scope limits that rule out a fair amount of the use the SEO pages imply
Three months old (domain registered 2026-07-17) with no independent hands-on review found: the visible footprint is a GitHub org with three repos, one directory review and a twelve.tools badge
Two endpoints the vendor's own OpenAPI schema documents - GET /v1/health and GET /v1/ready - return 404 on the live API, which is a small but concrete documentation defect for anyone integrating
No public affiliate or partner page (both routes drop to a sign-in screen), so there is no published referral terms to check
key_features: AI-phrasing rewrite of DOCX and PPTX with two strengths, returning the same editable format
Import an existing Turnitin or iThenticate AI report to rewrite only the flagged passages, or select passages yourself
Charged on words actually rewritten (100 credits per 1,000 words), with a free second pass on passages a fresh report still flags
Optional target word range (word_min / word_max) so the output lands inside a submission limit
Citation-format converter for APA 7, MLA 9, Harvard, IEEE, Chicago (author-date and notes), GB/T 7714, Vancouver, AMA, ACS and OSCOLA at 5 credits per 1,000 words
Document shortener to a word budget, whole-document or per-passage
Layout-preserving translator for 12 languages across PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, EPUB, HTML and plain text
Documented REST API (OpenAPI 3.1), MCP server and agent skill; credits usable in the app and the API
Waffo/Creem hosted checkout, one-time credit packs, credits that never expire, 100 free credits at signup
English and Chinese interfaces with the marketing site mirrored across 11 locales
faq: How much does HumanPen cost?

Credits are bought in one-time packs: 1,000 for USD 19, 5,000 for USD 79, 10,000 for USD 149 and 20,000 for USD 249, with a once-per-account first purchase at USD 9.90, 49, 98 and 196 respectively. New accounts start with 100 free credits. Humanizing costs 100 credits per 1,000 words actually rewritten, so the entry pack covers about 10,000 words at list price; citation-format correction is 5 credits per 1,000 words. Credits do not expire and there is no subscription - the Terms state each purchase is a one-time charge.
Is there a free trial?

Not a trial in the usual sense. Signing up grants 100 credits, worth about 1,000 words of humanizing or 20,000 words of citation correction, and that is enough to run a real short document through the pipeline. Beyond that it is pay-as-you-go; there is no time-limited trial and no money-back guarantee tied to a detector result - the vendor explicitly refuses to promise one.
Does it actually get past AI detectors?

The vendor declines to say so and we cannot verify it. There is no published pass rate, no third-party test, and HumanPen runs no detector of its own - it accepts the Turnitin or iThenticate report your institution issued instead, which is a more honest design than a self-graded score but still leaves the outcome dependent on a detector that changes. Judge it on your own document rather than on the category's usual 'guaranteed to pass' claims, which this vendor explicitly calls out as something it will not make.
What happens to my documents?

Uploaded documents and results are deleted 7 days after the job finishes, enforced by a scheduled sweep; job records such as file name, word counts and status stay with your account history until you delete the account, which the policy says happens within 30 days. Text is sent to third-party AI model providers for processing, and the policy states neither HumanPen nor those providers use it to train models. Order and payment records are kept 7 years for tax and accounting law.
Who is behind it, and where is it based?

That is not disclosed. Every page names only 'the HumanPen team'; there is no company, individual, country, postal address or company number, and the governing-law clause refers to 'the jurisdiction in which the HumanPen team operates' without naming one. Support runs through support@humanpen.net, which we confirmed is a working mailbox. Treat the identity gap as a real limitation if you need a counterparty with a legal address.
Can I use it for coursework?

Read your institution's rules first, because HumanPen's own Terms bar 'submitting work as your own where the substance of an assessment is required to be your independent work', and the /ethics page states that a processed manuscript still counts as AI-assisted where disclosure is required. The vendor markets the tool to students for exactly that coursework use, which is a genuine tension we would rather name than smooth over: the restriction is in the contract and the marketing points the other way.
trial_checklist: Start with the 100 free credits on a document you can afford to lose - a real one of a few hundred words, not a demo paragraph - and compare the output line by line against the input
Check the thing the vendor claims is protected: numbers, units, percentages, citations, figure numbering and any Word fields or cross-references, before and after
If you have a Turnitin or iThenticate report, import it rather than rewriting the whole file - that is the workflow the pricing is built around, and only the flagged passages are billed
Confirm the cost arithmetic before a large job: 100 credits per 1,000 words rewritten means the 20,000-word thesis is roughly 2,000 credits, i.e. the 5,000-credit pack, not the entry pack
Do not buy a big pack on a promise of passing a detector - there is none, and the vendor says so; buy the smallest pack that covers the document you actually have

Before uploading anything confidential, note that documents are sent to unnamed third-party model providers, kept 7 days, and that the site loads Google and Microsoft advertising tags with no consent control
If a job fails, watch that credits come back automatically - the Terms say a failed or cancelled job is never charged - and keep the order number support asks for
rating_rationale: Job fit 4.2/5 - the workflow is the right shape for the job: whole DOCX/PPTX in, same-format editable file out, metered on words actually rewritten, with a detection-report import that narrows the work and a free second pass. Four operations (rewrite, cite, condense, translate) share one credit balance, the API is published rather than promised, and the pricing ladder is one-time with credits that never expire. It is held below 4.5 by scope limits the vendor states itself (English-only humanizing, DOCX-only for two of the four operations, only two detectable report formats) and by effectiveness that cannot be verified from outside. Transparency 3.6/5 - the legal drafting is unusually good and mostly in the user's favour: output ownership retained, no training use, retention given as periods with the enforcement mechanism named, a specific 14-day unused-credit refund, and an /ethics page that concedes the product's real purpose instead of marketing around it. It scores 3.6 rather than higher because two things do not survive inspection: the cookie section claims only necessary session cookies and no advertising profiles while Google Ads and Microsoft Ads tags fire sitewide with no consent control and are absent from the processor list, and the governing-law clause names no jurisdiction at all while no company, person or address appears anywhere. Nothing here contradicts what the product does, which is why this lands at 3.9 rather than lower.

name: Money Tracker (Expense & Budget)

The middle pack is the one that makes sense if you plan to compare several styles. Not a fit for readers who want an anonymity-first try-on with no account and no stored history, who need a real fitting or prescription advice rather than a style preview, who want a free trial long enough to judge output on their own face, or who need a named company and a stated jurisdiction before paying.
price: One-time credit packs, no subscription: 10 credits USD 2.99, 30 credits USD 6.99 and 100 credits USD 14.99, each card showing a struck-through list price of USD 4.99 / 9.99 / 24.99. Credits never expire and each try-on costs 1 credit, so the packs buy 10, 30 or 100 generations; the per-credit arithmetic on the page reconciles (about USD 0.30, 0.23 and 0.15). Signup grants 1 credit, which is the entire free tier. The served plan payload marks every pack interval "one-time" with valid_days 0 and carries no recurring flag; the payment providers listed are Stripe and Creem. Verified 2026-10-25 from the rendered /pricing page and the plan payload embedded in it; the Chinese mirror /zh/pricing shows the same three packs at the same dollar prices.
summary: TryBestSpecs turns one selfie into a glasses try-on. The measuring step runs in the browser: the shipped bundle loads MediaPipe's FaceLandmarker with the GPU delegate, and its geometry feeds a face-shape classification (round, square, oval, heart, long, diamond) plus a skin-tone read that together drive the frame recommendations. Rendering the recommended frames onto your photo is a server-side AI step, and so is own-frame mode, where you upload a picture of frames you already own. Results land in an automatic history you can revisit, compare side by side, download in high resolution and share. Everything sits behind an account: signup grants 1 credit, each try-on costs 1 credit, and further credits come as one-time packs of 10, 30 or 100 that never expire. The interface, the guides and the legal pages are published in English and Chinese.
use_cases: Previewing rectangular, cat-eye, round, aviator, rimless and clear frames on your own photo before buying online or in a shop
Comparing several frames side by side from a single face analysis instead of re-uploading for each one
Trying frames you already own or have shortlisted, by uploading a picture of the frame itself in own-frame mode
Getting a second opinion by sharing a render before committing to a purchase
Chinese-speaking buyers: the whole funnel, including pricing and the legal pages, is mirrored at /zh
pros: The measuring pass really is client-side rather than merely described that way: the shipped bundle initialises MediaPipe's FaceLandmarker with the GPU delegate in the browser and feeds the resulting geometry into the classification, so the face measurement itself sends nothing. The two third-party fetches it needs (the WASM from cdn.jsdelivr.net and the model from storage.googleapis.com) carry no image.

The sale model is one-time and says so in machine-readable form, not just in copy: every pack in the served plan payload is interval "one-time" with valid_days 0 (never expires) and there is no recurring flag anywhere in the configuration.

The pricing arithmetic holds up: 30 credits at about USD 0.23 each and 100 at USD 0.15 both reconcile against the card prices, and the 1-credit-per-try-on rule is repeated consistently on the homepage, the pricing page, the FAQ and its structured data.

There is real editorial content behind the product: roughly 40 dated guides on face shapes, frame styles and try-on questions, published in both languages, which is what makes a recommendation like "browline frames for a long face" legible to someone who has never shopped by shape.

A legal set exists, is dated (Privacy Policy and Terms of Service both 28 April 2026) and both pages print the support address. That address is a live route, not decoration: the domain's own Cloudflare MX answers 250 for support@trybestspecs.com and 550 5.1.1 "Address does not exist" for a random local part, so it is a real mailbox and not a catch-all.

The Terms draw the medical line clearly - results are "for reference only" and "not medical, optometry, ophthalmology, or professional fitting advice" - and require the rights to any photo you upload, including other people's.
The product is narrow and describable in one sentence: no prompt box, no timeline, no editing suite and no upsell ladder beyond the three packs.
cons: The privacy promise on the page contradicts the product on the same page. The upload box says "Your photo and camera are used only for this try-on", and the FAQ - also emitted as FAQPage structured data - answers "Will my photo be saved?" with "Your photo is used only for this session's analysis and try-on generation. We don't use it for training or share it." Yet the same homepage advertises "History - Every try-on is saved automatically. Revisit, compare, and share with friends", the About page offers to "Save and compare different eyewear styles", the pricing page sells downloadable high-res renders, and the Privacy Policy retains information "for as long as reasonably necessary" and names "cloud databases, AI model providers, ... object storage" as processors. A face photo is precisely the input where session-only and retained are not the same offer.

Advertising and session-recording tags fire on every page, including the privacy policy itself, with no consent step: the root layout injects Google's gtag loader for Ads id AW-18136694057 and Microsoft Clarity project x12jqf0qok with strategy lazyOnload. The policy mentions only "necessary cookies" and unnamed "analytics tools", never Google Ads or Clarity, and the site carries no cookie or consent interface of any kind.

Training use is unstated where it matters: the word "train" appears nowhere in the Privacy Policy or the Terms, while the Terms grant a licence to process uploads "for providing, operating, maintaining, and improving the service" - broader than the FAQ's flat "we don't use it for training".

No operator identity and no governing law: no company, individual, country, postal address or company number appears on any fetched page, and the Terms contain no governing-law, jurisdiction, dispute or arbitration clause, so a buyer cannot see who the counterparty is or which law applies.

Processors are unnamed and retention has no period: the policy cites "third-party service providers such as cloud databases, AI model providers, email delivery services, payment providers, object storage, and analytics tools" without naming one, and retention is "as long as reasonably necessary" rather than a number of days.

Nothing states who owns the rendered try-on image. The Terms confirm you keep your uploads and protect the vendor's site, code, design and "AI workflow", but no clause assigns rights in the generated render.

There is no refund policy page (/refund-policy and /refunds both 404) and the Terms say consumed credits and "completed digital services" are "generally non-refundable", with no cooling-off or withdrawal statement for EU or UK buyers.

All three packs display a struck-through list price (USD 4.99, 9.99, 24.99) against a lower current price, so the discount is permanent rather than an offer; only the Starter card's "First-time pick" label hints at anything conditional.

The Chinese mirror mixes currencies - /zh/pricing shows the same dollar totals but quotes the per-credit cost in yuan (about 0.66 and 0.60) - and the shipped configuration also carries CNY amounts (9.9, 19.9, 59.9) that the page never displays.
The free tier is a single credit and the only samples are the vendor's own renders, so output quality on your own face cannot be judged before paying.

Privacy Policy and Terms both refer to "subscriptions" and "paid plans" as possible purchases although only one-time packs are sold, which leaves the sale model looser in the legal text than on the pricing page.
key_features: Selfie upload or in-browser camera capture, no app install
Face-shape classification across round, square, oval, heart, long and diamond, plus a skin-tone read used in the recommendations
AI render of recommended frames on your own photo, with side-by-side comparison of several styles
Own-frame mode: upload a picture of frames you already own and see them on your face
Automatic history - every try-on is saved and can be revisited, compared, downloaded in high resolution or shared

Bilingual interface and content in English and Chinese, pricing and legal pages included
Roughly 40 published eyewear guides covering face shapes and frame styles
faq: What does TryBestSpecs actually do?

It reads your face from one photo and puts glasses on it. MediaPipe face landmarks are measured in the browser, the site classifies your face shape and skin tone, recommends frame shapes and then renders those frames onto your photo with an AI model. You can compare several results side by side, try frames you already own in own-frame mode, and download or share a render. The output is a style preview - the Terms state it is not optometry or fitting advice.
How much does it cost?

One-time credit packs, no subscription: 10 credits for USD 2.99, 30 for USD 6.99 and 100 for USD 14.99, with list prices of USD 4.99 / 9.99 / 24.99 shown struck through. Each try-on costs 1 credit and credits never expire. Signup grants 1 credit, so there is one free try-on and no timed trial.
Will my photo be kept?

The site says two different things, and we record the contradiction rather than resolving it in the vendor's favour. The upload box says the photo is used only for this try-on and the FAQ says only for the session, but the same page advertises an automatic history you can revisit and share, and the Privacy Policy retains data "for as long as reasonably necessary" and passes it to unnamed AI model and storage providers. Assume the photo and the renders are stored until the vendor states a retention period.
Does it give optometry or prescription advice?

No, and the Terms say so plainly: results are "for reference only" and "not medical, optometry, ophthalmology, or professional fitting advice". It previews how a frame shape may look; it does not measure your prescription, pupillary distance or physical fit. Check real fit and lens requirements with an optician.
Who runs it, and what law applies?

No company, individual, country or postal address is published anywhere on the site, and the Terms name no governing law. The only contact is support@trybestspecs.com, which is a working mailbox. Treat the counterparty as unidentified until the operator says otherwise.
trial_checklist: Use the single free credit on the frame shape you are actually considering, not on the widest possible demo - the question worth answering is whether the render looks like you in that frame
Judge the render against a real photo of yourself wearing a similar frame, not against the vendor's showcase images, which are its own samples
Check the two things a flat overlay usually gets wrong: do the frames sit at your brow line and pupil height, and are the lens reflections and shadows plausible in your lighting
Download one render before you buy a pack, and confirm the file is the resolution you would actually show someone
If you plan to spend more than one pack, test own-frame mode on a frame you already own first - that is the workflow the product is really for, and it is where upload limits or bad cropping show up

Before paying, read the refund line in the Terms (consumed credits are non-refundable and there is no refund page) and decide whether a one-time purchase of 30 or 100 credits is safer than the entry pack
rating_rationale: Job fit 4.2/5 - the product is the right shape for the job: one photo in, several frame renders out, a client-side measurement pass that does not leak the photo, own-frame mode for frames you already own, and an automatic history to compare against. Pricing is one-time with credits that never expire, the per-credit arithmetic is honest, and roughly 40 dated guides give the recommendations something to stand on. It is held below 4.5 by scope (a style preview with no fit or prescription dimension), by a free tier of exactly one try-on, and by output quality that cannot be verified from outside without paying. Transparency 3.2/5, and this is what pulls the number to 3.7 rather than the 4.0+ the product would otherwise earn: a face-image tool tells users in its upload box and its structured-data FAQ that the photo is used only for that session and never shared, while the same page advertises an automatic saved history, the policy retains data indefinitely and hands it to unnamed model providers, and Google Ads plus Microsoft Clarity tags fire on the privacy policy itself with no consent step. Add no named controller, no governing law, no named processor, no retention period, no output-ownership clause and no refund page, and the documentation gap lands below the 3.8-4.2 band this catalog normally gives an unproven but real entrant - though well above a site whose pricing describes a different product, which is not the case here.
